summary: This informational document analyzes common security threats against the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) and their potential impacts on routing protocols that use it. It does not propose solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: NHDP uses HELLO messages to help wireless routers learn which routers are nearby. RFC 7186 describes attacks that can falsify this information and disrupt routing, but does not propose solutions.

subtitle: Threats to neighborhood information used by routing protocols in mobile ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: NHDP routers use HELLO messages to learn about nearby routers, but NHDP does not define built-in protection for the integrity of that information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes attacks on HELLO exchanges and describes how incorrect neighbor information can harm routing and flooding protocols that use NHDP.
tldr.outcome: The document proposes no solutions and points to RFC 7185 for integrity protection. RFC 7186 has been updated by RFC 7985.

today: RFC 7186 is an Informational threat analysis and has been updated by RFC 7985. It does not specify a protocol or propose solutions.

sections.title: Why NHDP Has Security Threats
sections.content:
The Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) lets routers learn about one-hop and two-hop neighbors through periodic HELLO messages. Routing protocols such as OLSRv2 and Simplified Multicast Forwarding use this information.

NHDP is often used in wireless networks, where devices in radio range can receive and send signals. The protocol does not define explicit measures to protect the integrity of the information it learns. RFC 7186 analyzes attacks and misconfigurations but does not propose solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless routers use HELLO messages to learn about nearby routers. If a message is false or missing, other routing protocols may make decisions using an incorrect network picture.

sections.title: The Attacker and HELLO Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines an attacker as a device in the network that intentionally tries to compromise NHDP information. A compromised NHDP router can send validly formatted control messages that add or omit information compared with a legitimate router.

Routers send HELLO messages by link-local multicast with a hop limit of 1, so these messages are not forwarded. HELLO messages report addresses as heard, symmetric, or lost neighbors. An attacker can provide false identity or link information or replay previously sent messages.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can send a correctly formatted HELLO that contains false neighbor information. HELLO messages reach only devices on the local link, but those devices use them to build their neighbor records.

sections.title: Attacks on Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
The RFC describes jamming, denial of service, eavesdropping, identity spoofing, link spoofing, replay, timing attacks, indirect channel overloading, and attacks on link-quality updates. These attacks can block messages, reveal topology, fill neighbor sets, or make a real link appear unreliable.

For example, a compromised router can claim another router's address, advertise a link that does not exist, or omit a real neighbor. It can also replay a legitimate HELLO from another place or time. An integrity check alone does not stop a replay of a message whose check was correctly calculated.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can block HELLO messages, watch them, claim false identities, invent links, repeat old messages, or provide misleading timing information. Each method can make routers record a different neighborhood.

sections.title: Effects on Routing and Flooding
sections.content:
Protocols that use NHDP may calculate multipoint relays (MPRs) from incorrect one-hop and two-hop information. A false neighbor report can prevent some routers from being selected to forward flooded messages, or cause a compromised router to be selected and then drop or alter traffic.

Incorrect information can also cause a broadcast storm, routing loops, invalid paths, or a data sinkhole. In a sinkhole, traffic for a destination may be sent to a compromised router instead of the real destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrong neighbor records can stop control messages from reaching part of a network or send traffic through an attacker. They can also create loops or make every neighbor relay the same traffic.

sections.title: Mitigations Mentioned for Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC does not propose solutions, but it identifies areas for future work. RFC 7185 adds integrity check values to HELLO messages, which can help admit trusted routers and protect against some attacks when routers are not compromised.

The RFC notes that integrity checks do not encrypt HELLO messages, do not prevent all replay, and do not solve false information from a compromised router. It mentions possible work on link metrics, time synchronization, nonces, and protecting routers and keys.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC describes risks rather than fixes. It points to integrity checks as one protection, while noting that checks do not hide messages or make a compromised router trustworthy.
